title: Tamales de Rajas
subtitle: cheese and poblano strip tamales steamed in corn husks
excerpt: Tamales de rajas are masa parcels filled with roasted poblano strips and melting cheese, wrapped in soaked corn husks and steamed until the dough is set and pulls cleanly from the husk. They take time but most of it is hands-on in a satisfying way. Making a large batch is the traditional approach.
sourceNotes: Tamales are one of the oldest foods in the Americas, with a history stretching back at least 8,000 years. They were consumed by Aztec, Maya and Inca civilisations, and remain central to Mexican celebrations and family cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked tamales for up to 3 months. Steam from frozen for 20 minutes to reheat.
recipe.batchNotes: Tamal-making is traditionally done in large groups. Double or triple the recipe easily.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fine flour made from nixtamalised maize. It is the base for tamales and corn tortillas. The word masa means dough in Spanish.
A traditional Mesoamerican dish made from masa dough wrapped around a filling, then enclosed in a corn husk or banana leaf and steamed until set.

content.text: This recipe yields 12 tamales and takes about 2 hours 30 minutes from start to finish. Soak the corn husks for at least 30 minutes before you begin so they are pliable enough to fold without splitting.

content.text: Roast and peel the poblanos. Hold each one over a gas flame or under a hot grill until the skin is blistered and blackened all over. Transfer to a bowl, cover with cling film and leave to steam for 15 minutes. Rub off the skins, remove the seeds and cut the flesh into strips about 1 cm wide. Set aside.
Make the masa dough. Beat the lard in a large bowl with a hand mixer or stand mixer for 3 to 4 minutes until light and fluffy. Add the

and 1 teaspoon of salt. Mix briefly to combine. Gradually add 350 to 400 ml of warm chicken stock, a little at a time, mixing until the dough holds together and feels like thick peanut butter. A good test: drop a small ball of dough into a glass of cold water. If it floats, there is enough fat. If it sinks, beat in a little more lard.

Drain the soaked corn husks and pat them dry. Lay one husk flat with the pointed end facing away from you. Spread about 3 tablespoons of masa dough onto the centre of the husk in a rough rectangle, leaving a 2 cm border on each side and the pointed end bare.

Fold the sides of the corn husk over the masa, then fold the bottom up. The tamale should be closed on three sides. Stand it upright in the steamer with the open end at the top. Pack them together so they hold each other up.

Fold one long edge of the husk over the filling so the masa meets itself and encloses the filling completely. Fold the other long edge over the top. Fold the pointed end up to seal the bottom. The open top can remain open, or tie with a thin strip of torn husk. Repeat with all 12 husks.

Stand the tamales upright in a steamer basket with the open ends facing up. They should be packed snugly so they support each other. Steam over boiling water for 1 hour 15 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes. Check the water level halfway and top up if needed.
Test one tamale by unfolding the husk. The masa should be firm, set and pull away cleanly. If it sticks, reseal and steam for a further 15 minutes. Leave to rest for 5 minutes before serving.

attrs.symptom: The masa is dense and gummy after steaming.
attrs.cause: Not enough fat was beaten into the dough, or the dough was too wet.
attrs.fix: The float test in step 2 is the most reliable check. If dough sinks, mix in more lard before assembling.

attrs.symptom: The corn husks split when folding.
attrs.cause: The husks were not soaked long enough and are still stiff.
attrs.fix: Soak for at least 30 minutes in very hot water. Husks should be soft and flexible before you begin.

attrs.symptom: The filling leaks out during steaming.
attrs.cause: The masa layer was spread too thin at the edges, or the tamale was not sealed tightly.
attrs.fix: Make sure the masa rectangle has no gaps at the edges and that the long sides overlap completely when folded.

content.text: Tamales are made across Mexico and most of Latin America. They are celebration food, made in large quantities with family helping. The rajas and cheese filling is one of the most popular versions in central Mexico. Once you have made a batch, reheating from the freezer is quick and easy.
